title: The Conversion of Saint Paul (25 January)
hook: the unity week ends with the Damascus road

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wattson, and a week of prayer running from Peter's feast to Paul's. Your line was that they may be one.

Look at the famous paintings of this scene, Caravaggio's for one, and you'll see a man flat on his back in the dirt, arms thrown up, and a huge horse standing over him. It's the picture that stuck: Paul knocked off his horse. But Acts never mentions a horse, not once in the three times the story is told. The artists added it. What Acts does give us is stranger than a fall from a saddle, and the unity week ends on it.
screen: `FLAT ON HIS BACK.` → `NO HORSE IN ACTS.` → `STRANGER THAN A FALL.`

segments.voice: Saul of Tarsus was a Pharisee, zealous for his tradition and certain that the followers of Jesus were a danger to it. He had stood by at Stephen's death. Now he carries letters from the high priest to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. Near the city, a light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Not my followers. Me. Saul asks, "Who art thou, Lord?" And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Some readers hear in that word a seed of what Paul would later write: the Church as the body of Christ, so what is done to its members is done to him. Saul gets up blind. His companions lead him by the hand into the city, the hunter now helpless, and for three days he neither eats nor drinks. Then the Lord sends a disciple named Ananias, who objects: he has heard how much harm this man has done, and why he has come. He goes anyway, lays hands on him, and calls him brother Saul. Something like scales fall from Saul's eyes, and he is baptized. One more correction: the conversion doesn't rename him. Acts keeps calling him Saul for several more chapters; only later, on his travels, does it say Saul, who is also called Paul. His conversion has its own feast, and it closes the unity week: the man who set out to break up the community spends the rest of Acts building it.
screen: `LETTERS TO DAMASCUS.` · `WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · `BLIND, LED BY THE HAND.` · `ANANIAS SAYS, BROTHER.` · then, large: `I AM JESUS WHOM THOU PERSECUTEST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone headed the wrong way, an angry relative, a friend in trouble, a public figure who frightens you, and instead of rehearsing what they've done, picture them on a road with a light reaching them. Then think of Ananias, who had to go and call his enemy brother. If you pray, pray for that person to turn and for yourself to be ready when they do; if not, simply wish them a road back.
Ananias, the disciple. Sent to the blinded Saul in Damascus, frightened but obedient, the one who called him brother and healed his eyes. Today's word.
Your line: the persecutor turned. Ananias kept the door open. Day six hundred forty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Catholics keep January 25 as the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, which also closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, often with an ecumenical Vespers in Rome at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul fell off his horse and got a new name.
what it means: a persecutor met the risen Jesus on the Damascus road, was blinded, welcomed by Ananias and baptized.
what a scholar hears: Acts tells it three times (9, 22, 26) with no horse; 'me' in 9:4 anticipates Paul's body-of-Christ teaching, and the name Paul appears only at 13:9.

chat.says: On the road to Damascus, what actually happened to Paul?
options: Acts tells of a light, a voice from heaven, and Saul falling to the ground, blinded.
Acts says he was struck by lightning and lost his hearing for a week.
Acts says the high priest's guards turned him back before he reached the city.
chat.meaning: Acts tells it three times: a light, a fall to the ground, a voice, and blindness until Ananias came. The name Paul comes chapters later.

Caravaggio.meaning: an Italian painter whose version of the scene shows a horse

Pharisee.meaning: a member of a Jewish group zealous for the law

Damascus.meaning: the city where Saul set out to arrest believers
